summary: Defines the Message Bus (Mbus), a lightweight protocol for local coordination between application components. It provides automatic discovery of peers, subject-based addressing and reliable messages, and uses IP multicast. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs on one computer or network need to chat. This is a shared group chat where they can find each other and send messages to a topic.

subtitle: A lightweight protocol for coordinating independent application components on the same network.

tldr.problem: When multiple application components run on the same host or network (such as separate audio, video and UI tools in a conferencing system), they need a way to discover each other and coordinate without complex middleware.
tldr.mechanism: Mbus provides automatic peer discovery, subject-based message addressing, reliable and unreliable delivery modes, and security mechanisms, all layered on top of IP multicast with limited scope (same link or host only).
tldr.outcome: Components can be loosely coupled yet coordinated, making it easy to build flexible conferencing systems and other multi-component applications where tools can work independently or together.

today: RFC 3259 is an Informational document from 2002. Mbus was designed for local coordination in multimedia conferencing systems, particularly within the MBone (multicast backbone) research community. While the RFC remains the authoritative specification, Mbus has seen limited widespread adoption outside academic and research environments. The principles it embodies—automatic peer discovery, subject-based addressing, and lightweight message passing—influenced later local coordination systems and are reflected in modern technologies like mDNS for service discovery and local pub/sub systems.

sections.title: What is Mbus and Why It Exists
sections.content:
Mbus (Message Bus) is a lightweight, message-oriented protocol for group communication between application components on the same host or local network. Published in April 2002, it addresses a real problem in systems like multimedia conferencing: separate tools (audio engine, video engine, user interface, whiteboard, etc.) need to coordinate without being tightly coupled to one another.

In multimedia conferencing systems, a typical architecture uses separate tools to handle audio, video and shared workspaces. Each tool is independent and can be started or stopped without affecting others, but they need to communicate to synchronize media, coordinate shared resources like input devices, and respond together to user commands. Similarly, Internet appliances or device groups connected to a local network need local coordination without complex configuration.

Mbus solves this by providing a simple, standardized coordination infrastructure. It uses IP multicast limited to a single link or host (not routable across the Internet), assigns communication addresses based on hierarchical tags and values, and supports both reliable and unreliable message delivery depending on what each message needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine separate programs for sound, video, and text all running on the same computer. They need to know about each other and send messages back and forth. Mbus is the system that lets them do that automatically.

sections.title: Addressing and Discovery
sections.content:
Mbus uses a flexible addressing scheme where each entity is identified by a set of tag:value address elements. For example, an audio engine in a conference might have the address:

(conf:test media:audio module:engine app:rat id:4711-1@192.168.1.1)

This address says that the entity belongs to conference 'test', handles 'audio' media, is a 'module' that is an 'engine', comes from the 'rat' application, and has a unique identifier of '4711-1@192.168.1.1' (process ID-disambiguator at the IP address).

A message can be sent to any subset of address elements. A message to (media:audio module:engine) reaches all audio engines regardless of conference or application. A message to (module:engine) reaches all engines. An empty address reaches all entities on the Mbus.

Every Mbus entity announces its presence with hello messages when starting up, and periodically throughout its lifetime. This allows other entities to discover newcomers and detect when entities leave or fail. The hello message frequency adapts dynamically based on the number of known entities, scaling gracefully as sessions grow.
sections.plainLanguage: Each program gets a name made of different tags, like 'audio engine' or 'video engine'. You can send messages to one program, to all programs of one type, or to everyone. Programs say 'hello' when they start so everyone knows they're there.

sections.title: Messages and Transport
sections.content:
Every Mbus message has a header and a body. The header includes:

A protocol identifier ('mbus/1.0') marking the version. A sequence number that increments with each message sent by an entity, allowing recipients to detect lost or duplicate messages. A timestamp in milliseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC. A message type field indicating 'R' for reliable (acknowledged) or 'U' for unreliable. The source address and destination address, where the destination may be incomplete to match multiple recipients. An ack list containing sequence numbers being acknowledged.

The body contains zero or more commands in a simple syntax: a command name followed by zero or more typed parameters (integers, floats, strings, lists, symbols, or opaque binary data encoded in base64). Command names use hierarchical dot-separated notation like mbus.hello or app.ui.set-volume.

Messages are transmitted as UDP datagrams. Local multicast or broadcast is used to reach all or multiple recipients (link-local or host-local scope determined by TTL). Optional directed unicast may be used to send directly to a single known entity. The registered Mbus UDP port is 47000. Messages are limited to 64 kilobytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a header that says where it's from, where it's going, whether it needs an answer, and the time. Then there's the actual message, which is a command with some data attached. Messages go over the network using multicast.

sections.title: Reliability and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
Not all messages need guaranteed delivery. Transient state information (like an audio level meter) can be sent unreliably—if one message is lost, the next one will update the value. But messages that change conference state or configure components must be delivered reliably.

The Mbus supports reliable messages for point-to-point communication to a fully qualified destination address. When a sender transmits a reliable message, it keeps a copy and starts a timer (initialized to 100 milliseconds). The receiver must acknowledge within 70 milliseconds by including the message's sequence number in an ack list on a message back to the sender (either a dedicated ack message or piggybacked onto another message). If the sender's timer expires without an acknowledgment, it retransmits the message with a longer timeout. After three retransmission attempts, the sender gives up and notifies the application that delivery failed.

Reliable delivery is not allowed for multicast messages (one-to-many), keeping the protocol simple. If an application needs reliable delivery to multiple recipients, it sends individual reliable messages to each fully qualified address.
sections.plainLanguage: Some messages are important and need a promise that they arrived. The receiver sends back an 'I got it' message. If the sender doesn't hear back quickly, it sends again. Important messages try three times before giving up.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
Because Mbus messages are multicast or broadcast on the local network, they could be seen or spoofed by other users or malicious applications. The RFC defines a security framework to prevent this.

Message authentication: Every Mbus message can carry a message authentication code (MAC) computed over the message using a shared secret. This proves the message came from an authenticated entity and has not been modified.

Encryption: Messages can optionally be encrypted using a secret key algorithm to protect privacy and ensure the Mbus can be used for sensitive purposes like local key distribution.

Configuration parameters for each Mbus session (encryption keys, shared secrets, multicast addresses, TTLs) are stored in a configuration file or registry. Entities participating in the same Mbus session must be configured with the same security parameters.

The RFC explicitly notes that Mbus is designed for local coordination (same host or link), not for Internet-scale communication. Its security model assumes that entities on the same link are less likely to be malicious, and that administrators control Mbus configuration. It does not attempt to solve the key distribution problem in a large-scale open network.
sections.plainLanguage: On a shared network, other programs could try to fake messages. Each message can carry a secret code to prove it came from the right place. Messages can also be encrypted to keep them private.

sections.title: Application Scenarios
sections.content:
The Mbus enables several classes of applications.

Multimedia conferencing: Loosely coupled conference tools can coordinate through Mbus while maintaining independence. A central conference controller can use Mbus to enforce conference-wide control. Media synchronization (lip sync between audio and video) can be implemented via Mbus without changing the media tools themselves. Floor control (who can talk or draw) can be managed across tools.

Distributed system components: An IP telephone can be dynamically extended to include additional media engines (whiteboard, screen share, etc.) by discovering them via Mbus and coordinating through Mbus commands. Different vendors' tools can be combined to build a coherent system for a single user.

Device coordination: Home appliances or office devices connected to a local network can discover each other and coordinate actions without manual configuration. A system bus allows devices to announce capabilities and respond to requests.

Monitoring and control: Separate components can report status (audio level, video frame rate, network quality) to a UI component via unreliable Mbus messages. The UI stays synchronized with real-time state without being tightly coupled to every component that produces state.
sections.plainLanguage: Different programs can use Mbus to coordinate meetings on a conference call, to let a phone add features on the fly, to let home gadgets talk to each other, or to keep a dashboard updated with live information.
